Graded Keller maps and the Jacobian Conjecture

T. Shaska
Date: August 24, 2026
Abstract.

Rational points on weighted projective spaces are sparse: a point of ℙn​(ℚ)\mathbb{P}^{n}(\mathbb{Q}) lifts along the Veronese morphism only when a Kummer condition holds at every prime [9]. We ask what this viewpoint says about the Jacobian Conjecture. The map recently announced as a counterexample is equivariant for the grading 𝐰𝐭⁡(x,y,z)=(1,−1,−2)\mathbf{wt}(x,y,z)=(1,-1,-2), and we show that the sign pattern of such a grading decides everything. If the weights are all positive, the setting of weighted projective spaces, an equivariant Keller map is always an automorphism, so no counterexample can be graded that way. In dimension two the same holds for every sign pattern. The Keller condition itself descends to the quotient, where it says that the Jacobian of the quotient map vanishes to order two along the contracted locus. Over ℚ\mathbb{Q} the image of the counterexample is a thin set. But along the line where the group action has stabilizer μ2\mu_{2}, the two preimages on the contracted locus are rational exactly when −a-a is a square, so the Kummer condition of the positive-weight theory reappears on the stacky stratum. We propose a classification of equivariant polynomial maps by the signature of the weights, with weighted projective geometry as the positive case.

1. Introduction

In July 2026, L. Alpöge announced a counterexample to the Jacobian Conjecture in dimension three, credited to the AI system Fable [1]. Writing F=(a,b,c):ℂ3→ℂ3F=(a,b,c)\colon\mathbb{C}^{3}\to\mathbb{C}^{3} for the map

(1) a\displaystyle a =(1+x​y)3​z+y2​(1+x​y)​(4+3​x​y),\displaystyle=(1+xy)^{3}z+y^{2}(1+xy)(4+3xy),
b\displaystyle b =y+3​x​(1+x​y)2​z+3​x​y2​(4+3​x​y),\displaystyle=y+3x(1+xy)^{2}z+3xy^{2}(4+3xy),
c\displaystyle c =2​x−3​x2​y−x3​z,\displaystyle=2x-3x^{2}y-x^{3}z,

we have detJ​F≡−2\det JF\equiv-2, while FF is generically three-to-one. The components of FF are homogeneous with respect to a nonstandard grading. This was observed independently and earlier in [3, 8], in the opposite sign convention 𝐰𝐭⁡(x,y,z)=(−1,1,2)\mathbf{wt}(x,y,z)=(-1,1,2), as were versions of some results of Sec. 4 and Sec. 5; we learned of this after the present analysis was under way, and give independent proofs of everything we use.

Our own interest in Eq. 1 comes from a different direction. In [9] we studied rational points on weighted projective spaces 𝕎​ℙ𝐪n\mathbb{WP}^{n}_{\mathbf{q}}, and in particular the failure of the Veronese morphism φ:𝕎​ℙ𝐪n→ℙn\varphi\colon\mathbb{WP}^{n}_{\mathbf{q}}\to\mathbb{P}^{n} to be surjective on them: a rational point of ℙn\mathbb{P}^{n} lifts only when a Kummer condition holds at every prime, and for well-formed weights the liftable points have density zero. Sparsity of this kind is the ordinary behavior of a dominant polynomial map on rational points, not an exception to be explained; the Jacobian Conjecture asserted that a single algebraic identity on the differential rules it out globally. The grading of Eq. 1 makes it natural to ask how the two settings are related. The answer is that they are separated by the sign of the weights, and that the separation is a theorem rather than a technicality.

What we prove is the following. If the weights are all positive, which is the setting of weighted projective spaces, then an equivariant Keller map is an automorphism (Thm 3.2); a graded counterexample must therefore have weights of mixed sign, and Eq. 1 realizes the smallest such case.

In dimension two no signature admits a counterexample at all (Thm 3.3). The Keller condition itself descends to the invariant quotient, where it says that the Jacobian of the quotient map vanishes to order two along the contracted locus (Thm 6.1), reducing the problem for hyperbolically graded maps of ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n} to a degenerate Jacobian problem in dimension n−1n-1. Over ℚ\mathbb{Q} the image of Eq. 1 is a thin set, so a generic rational point has no rational preimage although over ℂ\mathbb{C} almost every point has three. Along the line where the action on the target has stabilizer μ2\mu_{2}, however, the two preimages on the contracted locus are rational exactly when −a-a is a square (Rem 5.3): the Kummer obstruction of the positive-weight theory reappears inside the hyperbolic example, on the stratum where the stabilizer is nontrivial. We close by proposing a classification of equivariant polynomial maps by the signature of the weights, of which [9] is the positive-weight case.

2. The grading

Let F=(a,b,c):ℂ3→ℂ3F=(a,b,c)\colon\mathbb{C}^{3}\to\mathbb{C}^{3} denote the map Eq. 1 throughout. Assign 𝐰𝐭⁡(x,y,z)=(1,−1,−2)\mathbf{wt}(x,y,z)=(1,-1,-2), so that x​yxy and x2​zx^{2}z have weight 00. Each component of FF is weight-homogeneous, of degrees deg⁡a=−2\deg a=-2, deg⁡b=−1\deg b=-1, and deg⁡c=1\deg c=1. Equivalently, with

σt​(x,y,z)=(t​x,t−1​y,t−2​z) and τt​(a,b,c)=(t−2​a,t−1​b,t​c),\sigma_{t}(x,y,z)=(tx,\,t^{-1}y,\,t^{-2}z)\quad\text{ and }\quad\tau_{t}(a,b,c)=(t^{-2}a,\,t^{-1}b,\,tc),

we have

(2) F∘σt=τt∘F(t∈𝔾m).F\circ\sigma_{t}=\tau_{t}\circ F\qquad(t\in\mathbb{G}_{m}).

The grading is unique up to scaling: the three monomials of cc alone force the weight vector to be a multiple of (1,−1,−2)(1,-1,-2), so it is an invariant of the map.

Lemma 2.1.

Let G:ℂn→ℂnG\colon\mathbb{C}^{n}\to\mathbb{C}^{n} be a polynomial map, equivariant for weighted 𝔾m\mathbb{G}_{m}-actions with source weights w1,…,wnw_{1},\dots,w_{n} and target degrees d1,…,dnd_{1},\dots,d_{n}; that is,

G⁡(tw1​x1,…,twn​xn)=(td1​G1​(x),…,tdn​Gn​(x))(t∈𝔾m).G\bigl(t^{w_{1}}x_{1},\dots,t^{w_{n}}x_{n}\bigr)=\bigl(t^{d_{1}}G_{1}(x),\dots,t^{d_{n}}G_{n}(x)\bigr)\qquad(t\in\mathbb{G}_{m}).
  1. (1)

    detJ​G\det JG is weight-homogeneous of weight ∑dj−∑wi\sum d_{j}-\sum w_{i}; if detJ​G\det JG is a nonzero constant, then ∑dj=∑wi\sum d_{j}=\sum w_{i}.

  2. (2)

    If all wiw_{i} and djd_{j} are nonzero, then G⁡(0)=0G(0)=0, and ∂Gj/∂xi​(0)=0\partial G_{j}/\partial x_{i}(0)=0 unless dj=wid_{j}=w_{i}.

Proof.

Write σt​(x)=(tw1​x1,…,twn​xn)\sigma_{t}(x)=(t^{w_{1}}x_{1},\dots,t^{w_{n}}x_{n}). Differentiating the equivariance in xx gives J​G​(σt​p)​diag⁡(tw1,…,twn)=diag⁡(td1,…,tdn)​J​G​(p),JG(\sigma_{t}p)\,\operatorname{diag}(t^{w_{1}},\dots,t^{w_{n}})=\operatorname{diag}(t^{d_{1}},\dots,t^{d_{n}})\,JG(p), and hence

detJ​G​(σt​p)=t∑dj−∑wi​detJ​G​(p),\det JG(\sigma_{t}p)=t^{\sum d_{j}-\sum w_{i}}\det JG(p),

which proves (1).

Setting x=0x=0 in the equivariance gives tdj​Gj​(0)=Gj​(0)t^{d_{j}}G_{j}(0)=G_{j}(0) for all tt; since dj≠0d_{j}\neq 0, this forces Gj​(0)=0G_{j}(0)=0, so G⁡(0)=0G(0)=0. Finally, the entry ∂Gj/∂xi\partial G_{j}/\partial x_{i} is homogeneous of weight dj−wid_{j}-w_{i}, and evaluating the corresponding scaling identity at the fixed point 00 gives

∂Gj/∂xi​(0)=tdj−wi​∂Gj/∂xi​(0)\partial G_{j}/\partial x_{i}(0)=t^{\,d_{j}-w_{i}}\,\partial G_{j}/\partial x_{i}(0)

for all tt, which forces the entry to vanish unless dj=wid_{j}=w_{i}. ∎

For Eq. 1 the degree vector (−2,−1,1)(-2,-1,1) is the reversal of the weight vector (1,−1,−2)(1,-1,-2), so ∑dj=∑wi=−2\sum d_{j}=\sum w_{i}=-2 and the linear part of FF at the origin is anti-diagonal: ∂a/∂z=1\partial a/\partial z=1, ∂b/∂y=1\partial b/\partial y=1, ∂c/∂x=2\partial c/\partial x=2. Since the reversal permutation on three letters is odd,

detJ​F=detJ​F​(0)=−(1⋅1⋅2)=−2.\det JF\;=\;\det JF(0)\;=\;-(1\cdot 1\cdot 2)\;=\;-2.

The constant −2-2 is the product of the three anti-diagonal leading coefficients.

Lemma 2.2.

Let GG be as in Lem 2.1 with detJ​G​(0)≠0\det JG(0)\neq 0. Then there is a permutation π\pi of {1,…,n}\{1,\dots,n\} with dj=wπ⁡(j)d_{j}=w_{\pi(j)} for all jj; if the wiw_{i} are pairwise distinct, π\pi is unique and J​G​(0)JG(0) is supported on the graph of π\pi.

Proof.

Expand

detJ​G​(0)=∑πsgn⁡(π)​∏j∂Gj/∂xπ⁡(j)​(0).\det JG(0)=\sum_{\pi}\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)\prod_{j}\partial G_{j}/\partial x_{\pi(j)}(0).

By Lem 2.1(2) each factor vanishes unless dj=wπ⁡(j)d_{j}=w_{\pi(j)}, so a nonzero determinant requires at least one permutation along which all the equalities hold. If the wiw_{i} are distinct, the condition dj=wπ⁡(j)d_{j}=w_{\pi(j)} determines π⁡(j)\pi(j), and every other entry of J​G​(0)JG(0) vanishes. ∎

In particular the multiset of target degrees of a graded Keller map equals the multiset of source weights, refining the identity ∑dj=∑wi\sum d_{j}=\sum w_{i} of Lem 2.1. For Eq. 1 the weights (1,−1,−2)(1,-1,-2) are distinct and π\pi is the reversal, which is the anti-diagonal linear part computed above.

3. Two cases of the Jacobian Conjecture

3.1. Positive weights in any dimension

Lemma 3.1.

Let G:X→YG\colon X\to Y be a proper local homeomorphism of locally compact Hausdorff spaces, with YY connected and XX nonempty. Then GG is a covering map with finite fibers.

Proof.

GG is closed: if A⊆XA\subseteq X is closed and y∈G⁡(A)¯y\in\overline{G(A)}, choose a compact neighborhood KK of yy; then G​(A∩G−1​(K))G(A\cap G^{-1}(K)) is compact, hence closed, and contains yy in its closure, so y∈G⁡(A)y\in G(A). Being open (local homeomorphism), closed, and nonempty onto the connected YY, the map GG is surjective. Each fiber G−1​(y)G^{-1}(y) is compact by properness and discrete because GG is a local homeomorphism, hence finite, say G−1​(y)={x1,…,xk}G^{-1}(y)=\{x_{1},\dots,x_{k}\}. Choose disjoint open sets Ui∋xiU_{i}\ni x_{i} mapped homeomorphically onto open sets Vi∋yV_{i}\ni y, and set

V=(⋂i=1kVi)∖G⁡(X∖⋃iUi),V=\Bigl(\bigcap_{i=1}^{k}V_{i}\Bigr)\setminus G\bigl(X\setminus\textstyle\bigcup_{i}U_{i}\bigr),

which is open since GG is closed, and contains yy. Then

G−1​(V)=⨆i(Ui∩G−1​(V)),G^{-1}(V)=\bigsqcup_{i}\bigl(U_{i}\cap G^{-1}(V)\bigr),

each piece mapping homeomorphically onto VV; so VV is evenly covered. ∎

Theorem 3.2.

Let G:ℂn→ℂnG\colon\mathbb{C}^{n}\to\mathbb{C}^{n} be a Keller map, equivariant for weighted 𝔾m\mathbb{G}_{m}-actions as in Lem 2.1, with wi>0w_{i}>0 and dj>0d_{j}>0 for all i,ji,j. Then GG is an automorphism.

Proof.

Write

σt​(x)=(tw1​x1,…,twn​xn) and τt​(q)=(td1​q1,…,tdn​qn)\sigma_{t}(x)=(t^{w_{1}}x_{1},\dots,t^{w_{n}}x_{n})\quad\text{ and }\quad\tau_{t}(q)=(t^{d_{1}}q_{1},\dots,t^{d_{n}}q_{n})

for the two actions, in this proof only. Since detJ​G\det JG is a nonzero constant, GG is étale, hence a local biholomorphism.

Step 1: G−1​(0)={0}G^{-1}(0)=\{0\}. By Lem 2.1, G⁡(0)=0G(0)=0. Suppose G⁡(p)=0G(p)=0 with p≠0p\neq 0. The orbit map t↦σt​(p)t\mapsto\sigma_{t}(p) is non-constant: σt​(p)=p\sigma_{t}(p)=p for all tt would force twi​pi=pit^{w_{i}}p_{i}=p_{i} for all tt and all ii, hence p=0p=0 as all wi>0w_{i}>0. But

G⁡(σt​p)=τt​G​(p)=τt​(0)=0,G(\sigma_{t}p)=\tau_{t}G(p)=\tau_{t}(0)=0,

so the infinite connected set {σt​(p):t∈𝔾m}\{\sigma_{t}(p):t\in\mathbb{G}_{m}\} lies in G−1​(0)G^{-1}(0), which is discrete because GG is étale — a contradiction.

Step 2: GG is proper in the Euclidean topology. Define

ρ⁡(x)=maxi⁡|xi|1/wi and ρ′​(q)=maxj⁡|qj|1/dj.\rho(x)=\max_{i}|x_{i}|^{1/w_{i}}\quad\text{ and }\quad\rho^{\prime}(q)=\max_{j}|q_{j}|^{1/d_{j}}.

For t∈ℝ>0t\in\mathbb{R}_{>0} we have

ρ⁡(σt​x)=t​ρ​(x) and ρ′​(τt​q)=t​ρ′​(q).\rho(\sigma_{t}x)=t\rho(x)\quad\text{ and }\quad\rho^{\prime}(\tau_{t}q)=t\rho^{\prime}(q).

The slice S={ρ=1}S=\{\rho=1\} is compact, and every p≠0p\neq 0 is σt​(p¯)\sigma_{t}(\bar{p}) with t=ρ⁡(p)t=\rho(p) and p¯=σ1/t​(p)∈S\bar{p}=\sigma_{1/t}(p)\in S. By Step 1, 0∉G⁡(S)0\notin G(S), so

δ:=minq∈G⁡(S)⁡ρ′​(q)>0\delta:=\min_{q\in G(S)}\rho^{\prime}(q)>0

by compactness. Let K⊆ℂnK\subseteq\mathbb{C}^{n} be compact and suppose pk∈G−1​(K)p_{k}\in G^{-1}(K) with |pk|→∞|p_{k}|\to\infty, so tk:=ρ⁡(pk)→∞t_{k}:=\rho(p_{k})\to\infty. Then

ρ′​(G⁡(pk))=ρ′​(τtk​G​(p¯k))=tk​ρ′​(G⁡(p¯k))≥tk​δ⟶∞,\rho^{\prime}\bigl(G(p_{k})\bigr)=\rho^{\prime}\bigl(\tau_{t_{k}}G(\bar{p}_{k})\bigr)=t_{k}\,\rho^{\prime}\bigl(G(\bar{p}_{k})\bigr)\ \geq\ t_{k}\,\delta\ \longrightarrow\ \infty,

contradicting G⁡(pk)∈KG(p_{k})\in K. Hence G−1​(K)G^{-1}(K) is bounded and closed, so compact, and GG is proper.

Step 3: conclusion. By Lem 3.1, GG is a finite covering map of ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n} by ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n}. The base is simply connected, so the covering is trivial; the total space is connected, so it has one sheet, and GG is bijective. An injective polynomial map ℂn→ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n}\to\mathbb{C}^{n} is an automorphism of ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n} with polynomial inverse [6]. ∎

By Lem 2.2 the hypothesis on the djd_{j} is automatic: the degrees of GG are a permutation of the weights. If instead all weights are negative, replacing tt by t−1t^{-1} on both sides returns to the case above. Positive weights are the setting of weighted projective spaces and their finite Veronese quotients; Thm 3.2 says the Jacobian Conjecture is trivially true there for graded maps. A graded counterexample is therefore forced into mixed-sign weights, and Eq. 1 realizes the minimal hyperbolic case (1,−1,−2)(1,-1,-2).

3.2. Dimension two, all signatures

In dimension two no signature admits a counterexample, and the classification is explicit.

Theorem 3.3.

Let G:ℂ2→ℂ2G\colon\mathbb{C}^{2}\to\mathbb{C}^{2} be a Keller map equivariant for a nontrivial algebraic 𝔾m\mathbb{G}_{m}-action on source and target. Then GG is an automorphism. More precisely, there are polynomial automorphisms φ,ψ\varphi,\psi of ℂ2\mathbb{C}^{2} such that both actions become diagonal, with source weights (w1,w2)(w_{1},w_{2}), and ψ∘G∘φ−1\psi\circ G\circ\varphi^{-1} is:

  1. (1)

    triangular, possibly after exchanging the two coordinates, if w1,w2w_{1},w_{2} have the same sign;

  2. (2)

    affine, if one weight vanishes;

  3. (3)

    linear, of the form (x,y)↦(a0​x,b0​y)(x,y)\mapsto(a_{0}x,b_{0}y) or (x,y)↦(a0​y,b0​x)(x,y)\mapsto(a_{0}y,b_{0}x), if the weights have opposite signs.

Proof.

Every algebraic 𝔾m\mathbb{G}_{m}-action on 𝔸2\mathbb{A}^{2} is linearizable by a polynomial automorphism [4], so we may choose φ,ψ\varphi,\psi making both actions diagonal. Since a polynomial automorphism has constant nonzero Jacobian,

G′:=ψ∘G∘φ−1G^{\prime}:=\psi\circ G\circ\varphi^{-1}

is again a Keller map, equivariant for diagonal actions as in Lem 2.1, and GG is an automorphism if and only if G′G^{\prime} is; so we may assume the actions are diagonal, with source weights (w1,w2)(w_{1},w_{2}) and target degrees (d1,d2)(d_{1},d_{2}). In each case below we use that a component of weight ww is a linear combination of the monomials xi​yjx^{i}y^{j} with i​w1+j​w2=wiw_{1}+jw_{2}=w. In cases (1) and (3) the weights are nonzero, so Lem 2.2 applies and the degree type is a permutation of the weight type; case (2) is handled directly.

(1) Replacing tt by t−1t^{-1} if necessary, assume 0<w1≤w20<w_{1}\leq w_{2} and write (p,q)=(w1,w2)(p,q)=(w_{1},w_{2}). Take first the identity degree type, so deg⁡a=p\deg a=p and deg⁡b=q\deg b=q. If xi​yjx^{i}y^{j} has weight pp and j≥1j\geq 1, then q≤j​q≤pq\leq jq\leq p, so p=qp=q and (i,j)=(0,1)(i,j)=(0,1); hence a=a0​xa=a_{0}x when p<qp<q, and aa is a linear form when p=qp=q.

If xi​yjx^{i}y^{j} has weight qq, then either (i,j)=(0,1)(i,j)=(0,1), or j=0j=0 and i​p=qip=q, which requires p|qp\mid q and gives i=q/pi=q/p. Hence b=b0​y+b1​xq/pb=b_{0}y+b_{1}x^{q/p}, the last term present only if p|qp\mid q. Thus

G⁡(x,y)=(a0​x,b0​y+b1​xq/p)G(x,y)=(a_{0}x,\;b_{0}y+b_{1}x^{q/p})

is triangular, with detJ​G=a0​b0\det JG=a_{0}b_{0}, and GG is an automorphism; for p=qp=q the map is linear and invertible. The transposition degree type gives the same monomials with the roles of aa and bb exchanged, hence a triangular map composed with the exchange of coordinates.

(2) Say (w1,w2)=(p,0)(w_{1},w_{2})=(p,0) with p>0p>0, after inverting the action if needed. Here the monomial xi​yjx^{i}y^{j} has weight i​pip, so each component has degree in p​ℤ≥0p\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}; by Lem 2.1(1) the degrees satisfy d1+d2=pd_{1}+d_{2}=p, whence {d1,d2}={p,0}\{d_{1},d_{2}\}=\{p,0\}. If deg⁡a=p\deg a=p and deg⁡b=0\deg b=0, the weight-pp monomials are x​yjxy^{j} and the weight-00 monomials are yjy^{j}, so a=x​A​(y)a=xA(y) and b=B⁡(y)b=B(y) and detJ​G=A​B′\det JG=A\,B^{\prime}. If instead deg⁡a=0\deg a=0 and deg⁡b=p\deg b=p, then a=A⁡(y)a=A(y), b=x​B​(y)b=xB(y) and detJ​G=−A′​B\det JG=-A^{\prime}B, whence G⁡(x,y)=(a1​y+c0,b0​x)G(x,y)=(a_{1}y+c_{0},\;b_{0}x). The case (0,q)(0,q) is symmetric.

The target invariant is aq​bp=m​Aq​Bpa^{q}b^{p}=m\,A^{q}B^{p}, so G¯\bar{G} is the self-map

of 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}, and

M′=Aq​Bp+m⁡(q​Aq−1​A′​Bp+p​Aq​Bp−1​B′)=Aq−1​Bp−1⋅detJ​G.M^{\prime}=A^{q}B^{p}+m\bigl(qA^{q-1}A^{\prime}B^{p}+pA^{q}B^{p-1}B^{\prime}\bigr)=A^{q-1}B^{p-1}\cdot\det JG.

Write α=deg⁡A\alpha=\deg A and β=deg⁡B\beta=\deg B. Since

deg⁡M=1+q​α+p​β≥1,\deg M=1+q\alpha+p\beta\geq 1,

the left side has degree q​α+p​βq\alpha+p\beta, while the right side has degree (q−1)​α+(p−1)​β(q-1)\alpha+(p-1)\beta because detJ​G\det JG is a nonzero constant. Hence α+β=0\alpha+\beta=0, so α=β=0\alpha=\beta=0 and

G⁡(x,y)=(a0​x,b0​y).G(x,y)=(a_{0}x,b_{0}y).

For the transposition degree type the same computation with a=y​A​(m)a=yA(m), b=x​B​(m)b=xB(m) and target invariant ap​bqa^{p}b^{q} gives

M′=−Ap−1Bq−1detJGM^{\prime}=-A^{p-1}B^{q-1}\det JG

and the identical degree count, so G⁡(x,y)=(a0​y,b0​x)G(x,y)=(a_{0}y,b_{0}x). ∎

A counterexample in the plane, if one exists, therefore carries no 𝔾m\mathbb{G}_{m}-equivariance at all. We discuss in Sec. 8 what separates this case from Eq. 1.

4. Descent and the fiber cubic

The invariant rings of the two actions are polynomial:

Remark 5.3 (A Kummer condition on the stacky line).

The action τ\tau has stabilizer μ2\mu_{2} exactly along the punctured line {b=c=0,a≠0}\{b=c=0,\ a\neq 0\}, and σ\sigma has stabilizer μ2\mu_{2} along {x=y=0,z≠0}\{x=y=0,\ z\neq 0\}. By Prop 5.2, for α∈ℚ×\alpha\in\mathbb{Q}^{\times} the two preimages of (α,0,0)(\alpha,0,0) lying on {L=0}\{L=0\} have x2=−14​αx^{2}=-\tfrac{1}{4\alpha}, so

#​F−1​(α,0,0)​(ℚ)={3,−α∈(ℚ×)2,1,otherwise,\#F^{-1}(\alpha,0,0)(\mathbb{Q})=\begin{cases}3,&-\alpha\in(\mathbb{Q}^{\times})^{2},\\ 1,&\text{otherwise,}\end{cases}

the point (0,0,α)(0,0,\alpha) occurring in either case. Liftability of a rational point along the μ2\mu_{2}-fixed line is thus governed by a square class, an obstruction of exactly the Kummer type that governs the positive-weight setting [9]. The announced collision is the member α=−14\alpha=-\tfrac{1}{4} of this family, and α=−1\alpha=-1, with preimages (±12,∓3,26)(\pm\tfrac{1}{2},\mp 3,26), is the next.

Remark 5.4.

The trace of every fiber equals 2=|detJ​F|2=|\det JF|, the same constant produced by the anti-diagonal linear part in Lem 2.1. Whether this is a general feature of Keller maps graded by this weight type, or an accident of Eq. 1, we do not know.

The identity detJ​F=−2\det JF=-2 is equivalent to a two-dimensional statement about F¯\bar{F} and the contracted line. The following holds for every equivariant map of this weight type, not only for Eq. 1.

In these coordinates GG is

(x,u,v)↦(x​Λ​(u,v),P⁡(u,v),Q⁡(u,v)),(x,u,v)\mapsto\bigl(x\Lambda(u,v),\,P(u,v),\,Q(u,v)\bigr),

with Jacobian Λ⋅Jacu,v⁡(P,Q)\Lambda\cdot\operatorname{Jac}_{u,v}(P,Q). The source change (x,y,z)→(x,u,v)(x,y,z)\to(x,u,v) has Jacobian ±x3\pm x^{3} and the target change (c,P,Q)→(a,b,c)(c,P,Q)\to(a,b,c) has Jacobian ±c−3=±(x​Λ)−3\pm c^{-3}=\pm(x\Lambda)^{-3}, whence

on a dense open set, hence everywhere. The displayed value for Eq. 1 is a direct computation through the coordinates of Lem 4.1: one finds

∂(P,Q)∂(s,L)=−2​L,∂(s,L)∂(e,L)=L,∂(e,L)∂(u,v)=−1.\frac{\partial(P,Q)}{\partial(s,L)}=-2L,\qquad\frac{\partial(s,L)}{\partial(e,L)}=L,\qquad\frac{\partial(e,L)}{\partial(u,v)}=-1.

∎

Remark 6.2.

Thm 6.1 explains the cancellation Eq. 4: it is the condition Jac=κ​Λ2\operatorname{Jac}=\kappa\Lambda^{2} made explicit. It also inverts into a recipe: to build an equivariant Keller map of this weight type, solve the two-dimensional problem Jacu,v⁡(P,Q)=κ​Λ2\operatorname{Jac}_{u,v}(P,Q)=\kappa\Lambda^{2} — a Jacobian problem with prescribed divisorial vanishing along the contracted line — and lift. More generally, it reduces the Jacobian problem for hyperbolically graded maps of ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n} to a degenerate Jacobian problem on the (n−1)(n-1)-dimensional quotient. We do not know whether the exponent 22 admits a uniform description in terms of the weights; this is the first question the reduction raises.

7. Arithmetic: the image on rational points is thin

Everything above is defined over ℚ\mathbb{Q}. If (x,y,z)∈ℚ3(x,y,z)\in\mathbb{Q}^{3}, then s=L​e∈ℚs=Le\in\mathbb{Q}; hence a point (a,b,c)∈ℚ3(a,b,c)\in\mathbb{Q}^{3} with c≠0c\neq 0 has a rational preimage if and only if the cubic Eq. 5 has a rational root with L≠0L\neq 0.

Corollary 7.1.

F⁡(ℚ3)F(\mathbb{Q}^{3}) is a thin set in the sense of Serre [7]. By Hilbert irreducibility, outside a thin set of rational points (a,b,c)∈ℚ3(a,b,c)\in\mathbb{Q}^{3} the fiber F−1​(a,b,c)F^{-1}(a,b,c) contains no rational point.

Proof.

The source ℂ3\mathbb{C}^{3} is irreducible and FF is dominant of degree 33 by Prop 4.3, so F⁡(ℚ3)F(\mathbb{Q}^{3}) is the image of the rational points of an irreducible variety under a generically finite map of degree greater than one; such images are thin by definition [7, §3.1]. The second statement is Hilbert’s irreducibility theorem applied to the cubic Eq. 5, which is irreducible over ℂ⁡(a,b,c)\mathbb{C}(a,b,c) by Prop 4.3(3). ∎

Over ℂ\mathbb{C} almost every point of the target has three preimages; over ℚ\mathbb{Q} almost none has any. The counterexample therefore fails bijectivity on ℚ\mathbb{Q}-points in both directions at once: rational collisions, and a thin image. It is instructive to compare with the lifting problem for the Veronese morphism φ:𝕎​ℙ𝐪n→ℙn\varphi\colon\mathbb{WP}^{n}_{\mathbf{q}}\to\mathbb{P}^{n} on weighted projective spaces [9]. There the weights are positive, φ\varphi is finite and ramified, and liftability of a rational point is an abelian condition: a torsor under roots of unity, classified by Kummer classes and detected by congruences at every prime. Here the weights are hyperbolic, FF is étale and non-proper, and liftability is the splitting of a nonabelian S3S_{3}-resolvent, with no torsor structure and no congruence criterion — except along the stabilizer locus, where Rem 5.3 shows the abelian condition returns.

8. Concluding remarks

The results above leave a picture with some proved edges and some open middle. We close by recording both: why the mechanism of Eq. 1 needs dimension three, what a counting theory over ℚ\mathbb{Q} would require, and how the two papers’ settings fit into one classification.

Thm 3.3 settles the graded case in dimension two, and the reason is a ramification count. On the quotient the map becomes a polynomial self-map of 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1} of some degree dd, whose critical divisor has degree exactly d−1d-1; the Keller condition forces that divisor to be Aq−1​Bp−1A^{q-1}B^{p-1}, of degree d−1−(deg⁡A+deg⁡B)d-1-(\deg A+\deg B), which is smaller unless AA and BB are constant. In dimension three no such accounting holds: the quotient is a surface, the quotient map is not proper, and its ramification divisor {L=0}\{L=0\} costs nothing, because over a general point of the discriminant the missing sheets escape to infinity rather than coming together (Prop 5.1). The mechanism behind Eq. 1 needs somewhere for ramification to go, and a curve has nowhere. This also suggests where to look for structure we have not examined: the two GIT chambers of the hyperbolic action, of which we have used only {x≠0}\{x\neq 0\}, and whose other chamber appears related to the weighted projective line ℙ⁡(1,2)\mathbb{P}(1,2); we have not pursued this.

Restricting Eq. 1 to {x=0}\{x=0\} gives (y,z)↦(z+4​y2,y, 0)(y,z)\mapsto(z+4y^{2},\,y,\,0), a Jonquières automorphism of the plane onto {c=0}\{c=0\}, so every rational point of {c=0}\{c=0\} lifts. In the counting function

Z(X)=#{(a,b,c)∈ℚ3:H≤X,F−1(a,b,c)∩ℚ3≠∅}Z(X)=\#\{(a,b,c)\in\mathbb{Q}^{3}:H\leq X,\ F^{-1}(a,b,c)\cap\mathbb{Q}^{3}\neq\emptyset\}

this stratum should dominate, much as coordinate strata dominate the counting problems of [9], while off the stratum the count is governed by the splitting of Eq. 5; one expects the exponent there to come from a linear program, as in the positive-weight setting, though we have proved nothing in this direction. Part of the difficulty is foundational: the weighted heights of [2, 9] require positive weights, the stacky height frameworks require properness, and Eq. 1 lives where both hypotheses fail. A height theory for hyperbolic quotients — a quotient height coupled with an orbit term — would let the problem be posed precisely, and seems to us the natural first step.

The settings of [9] and of this note are two chambers of one classification. For a 𝔾m\mathbb{G}_{m}-action the governing invariant is the position of 00 relative to the weights: all weights of one sign (the elliptic case) gives proper, finite, ramified quotient maps, where the obstruction to lifting a rational point is a Kummer condition [9]; a zero weight (the parabolic case) gives a cylinder factor; 00 strictly between weights (the hyperbolic case) gives non-proper quotients with contracted loci, where liftability is the splitting of a resolvent, in this example with nonabelian Galois group and thin image. In dimensions two and three every algebraic 𝔾m\mathbb{G}_{m}-action on affine space is linearizable [4, 5], so there the classification covers all actions. By Thm 3.2 the Jacobian problem is trivial in the elliptic case; by Thm 3.3, in dimension two it is trivial in every case; and Rem 5.3 shows a Kummer condition inside the hyperbolic example, on the line where the stabilizer is nontrivial, suggesting a stratification by stabilizer type rather than a dichotomy. What is missing is the arithmetic of this classification: a theory of lifting rational points along equivariant maps, organized by signature, of which [9] would be the elliptic case and the analysis above a first hyperbolic example. For a torus of higher rank the geometric side is classical — the invariant becomes the position of the origin relative to the convex hull of the weights, and the chambers form the GIT fan — so the arithmetic questions can at least be asked in that generality. We hope to return to this.
